questions.stem: Hatshepsut's Egypt depended on the annual flood of the Nile. Which statement about Egypt's geography is correct?
options: The Nile flowed from north to south, so Upper Egypt lay near the sea
Most Egyptians farmed the desert oases rather than the Nile valley
The cataracts of the Nile lay in the marshy Delta, close to the Mediterranean
The fertile Black Land along the river was bordered by the desert Red Land
questions.explanation: Egyptians called the fertile floodplain kemet (the Black Land) and the desert deshret (the Red Land). The Nile flows north, so Upper Egypt is in the south and the cataracts lie towards Nubia, not in the Delta.

questions.stem: In Egyptian ideology, the king's chief religious duty was to:
options: choose the high priests by consulting the oracle of Punt
maintain Ma'at by serving the gods and holding back chaos
lead the daily offering rites in every temple in person
write the funerary texts used in the tombs of officials
questions.explanation: The king stood between gods and people and was responsible for Ma'at, the right order of the world. Priests performed the daily rites in the king's name, since he could not be in every temple himself.

questions.stem: Before she became king, Hatshepsut held the title God's Wife of Amun. Why was this office important for her later rise?
options: It was the title given by law to whichever heir was chosen to succeed the king
It let her rule Lower Egypt alone while her husband ruled the south
It gave her a religious role, estates and close ties to the Amun priesthood
It made her the commander of the army garrisons stationed in Nubia
questions.explanation: The God's Wife of Amun took part in temple ritual and controlled property, giving Hatshepsut wealth, status and links with the priesthood of Amun at Karnak. It was not a title of succession or a military command.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's parents were:
options: Ahmose I and his queen, Ahmose-Nefertari
Thutmose I and his Great Royal Wife, Ahmose
Thutmose II and his secondary wife, Iset
Amenhotep I and his chief queen, Meritamun
questions.explanation: Hatshepsut was a daughter of Thutmose I and Queen Ahmose. Iset was the mother of Thutmose III, Hatshepsut's stepson and nephew.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut married Thutmose II, who was:
options: her cousin, the son of Amenhotep I by a Nubian princess
a general of non-royal birth chosen by the Amun priests
her uncle, a younger brother of her father Thutmose I
her half-brother, a son of Thutmose I by a lesser wife
questions.explanation: Thutmose II was a son of Thutmose I by Mutnofret, so he was Hatshepsut's half-brother. Marriage within the royal family strengthened his claim to the throne.

questions.stem: When Thutmose II died, his heir Thutmose III was a young child. What happened next?
options: Hatshepsut had Thutmose III exiled to Nubia and ruled entirely alone
Hatshepsut acted as regent and within a few years was crowned king
Hatshepsut ruled as regent until Thutmose III came of age, then retired
The vizier ruled Egypt for twenty years in the name of the young king
questions.explanation: Hatshepsut first ruled as regent for her stepson, and by about Year 7 of his reign she had taken the full titles of a king. Thutmose III was not removed: the two were co-rulers, with Hatshepsut as senior king.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's daughter, who was given a prominent role at court, was:
options: Neferure
Nefertari
Meritaten
Ankhesenamun
questions.explanation: Neferure appears on monuments with titles such as God's Wife of Amun, and Senenmut was her tutor. Nefertari was a queen of Ramesses II, and Meritaten and Ankhesenamun were daughters of Akhenaten.

questions.stem: On the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahri, the Divine Birth reliefs show the god Amun visiting Queen Ahmose in the form of Thutmose I, and Khnum shaping the child on his potter's wheel. What was the purpose of these scenes?
options: To record the public ceremonies held when she married Thutmose II at Thebes
To show the rites performed at the burial of her father
To prove that Thutmose III had no royal blood at all
To claim that Hatshepsut was the daughter of Amun and chosen to rule
questions.explanation: The Divine Birth cycle presented Hatshepsut as the physical child of Amun, which made her rule the god's will. Amenhotep III later used a similar birth cycle at Luxor, showing it was a royal theme rather than a unique invention.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's Coronation reliefs show her father Thutmose I presenting her to the court as his successor. Why do historians treat this scene with caution?
options: It contradicts the Divine Birth reliefs, which say she was crowned by Amun alone
It was carved by Thutmose III, who wished to show her as a usurper
It survives only in a copy made by a Greek historian under the Ptolemies
It was carved years later to justify her rule, and no earlier record confirms it
questions.explanation: The scene was created during Hatshepsut's own reign, after Thutmose II had ruled in between, so it served her claim. No document from Thutmose I's reign names her as his heir.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri was called Djeser-djeseru, meaning:
options: 'Mansion of the Aten'
'Horizon of Khufu'
'Holiest of Holies'
'House of Millions of Years'
questions.explanation: Djeser-djeseru means 'Holiest of Holies'. The temple was dedicated mainly to Amun, with shrines to Hathor and Anubis and a cult for Hatshepsut and her father.

questions.stem: Which feature of Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahri is distinctive?
options: A circle of standing stones aligned on the winter sunrise over the Nile
A hypostyle hall of 134 columns facing the temple of Luxor across the river
Rising terraces with colonnades set against the cliffs of the west bank
A single great pyramid built of limestone blocks over the burial chamber
questions.explanation: The temple's terraces and colonnades rise towards the cliffs, beside the older temple of Mentuhotep II, which partly inspired it. The famous 134-column hypostyle hall is at Karnak and was built much later.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's officials raised obelisks for her at Karnak. One still stands there today. What did such obelisks express?
options: A boundary marker showing the edge of the land owned by the Amun temple
The tomb of the king, since the burial chamber lay beneath the base
A record of tax collected, carved year by year on each of the four faces
Devotion to Amun-Ra and the king's power to quarry and move huge stones
questions.explanation: Obelisks were sacred to the sun god and their inscriptions dedicated them to Amun-Ra. Cutting single granite blocks at Aswan and moving them to Thebes also displayed the resources of the crown.

questions.stem: The Red Chapel (Chapelle Rouge) that Hatshepsut built at Karnak was:
options: a palace gateway where foreign tribute was presented to the king
a shrine for the sacred barque of Amun, built of red quartzite
a burial chapel for Senenmut, built from red Nubian sandstone
a granary for temple grain, painted red to ward off evil spirits
questions.explanation: The Red Chapel housed Amun's portable barque, and its reliefs show festivals and Hatshepsut's role in them. It was later dismantled and its blocks reused, and it has been reconstructed from them.

questions.stem: At the Speos Artemidos, a rock-cut temple near Beni Hasan for the lioness goddess Pakhet, Hatshepsut's inscription claims that she:
options: led the Egyptian army that drove the Hyksos out of the Delta in person
made Pakhet the chief god of Egypt in place of Amun of Thebes
was the first woman to rule Egypt since the time of the pyramids
restored what had been ruined since the Hyksos ruled in the north
questions.explanation: The text presents Hatshepsut as restoring temples and order after the Hyksos, who had been expelled before she was born. Linking herself to that victory helped show her as a king who upheld Ma'at.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut had a tomb cut in a remote cliff as a queen, but as king she was buried in KV20 in the Valley of the Kings. What does the change suggest?
options: Thutmose III ordered her burial moved after her death to dishonour her
Queens were forbidden by law from having their own tombs cut at Thebes
A king's burial needed a royal tomb in the valley, near that of her father
The cliff tomb was robbed before it was finished and had to be abandoned
questions.explanation: Her queen's tomb was not fit for a king, so she extended KV20, where her father Thutmose I was also buried. The change follows her new status as pharaoh.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt, recorded at Deir el-Bahri, was led by the official:
options: Nehesy
Senenmut
Ineni
Rekhmire
questions.explanation: The reliefs name Nehesy as the leader of the voyage. Senenmut was her steward and Ineni an architect of earlier kings, while Rekhmire was vizier under Thutmose III.

questions.stem: The Punt reliefs at Deir el-Bahri show the ruler of Punt, Parahu, and his wife Ati, as well as houses built on stilts. Why do historians value these scenes?
options: They are the only evidence that Hatshepsut led armies in person
They were painted by artists from Punt who came back to Thebes
They give rare detail on a distant land and on Egyptian trade by sea
They prove that Punt lay on the Mediterranean coast, close to the port of Byblos
questions.explanation: The reliefs depict people, plants, animals and dwellings of Punt and the loading of ships. Punt's exact location is still debated, but it lay to the south, reached via the Red Sea, not on the Mediterranean.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut placed the Punt expedition prominently on her temple. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: It shows that Egypt had conquered Punt and made it a province ruled by a vizier
It proves that she had no interest in military affairs during her whole reign
It presented peaceful trade for Amun's incense as a great achievement of her reign
It hid a military defeat in Nubia by replacing it with an invented voyage
questions.explanation: The myrrh brought back was used in Amun's cult, and the texts say the god himself commanded the voyage. Evidence of campaigns in Nubia shows she did not neglect military affairs, and Punt was never ruled by Egypt.

questions.stem: Older histories called Hatshepsut a peaceful ruler who neglected the army. More recent historians question this mainly because:
options: Greek historians describe her as Egypt's greatest warrior pharaoh
inscriptions point to campaigns in Nubia and perhaps the Levant in her reign
the annals of Thutmose III credit her with winning the Battle of Megiddo in person
her temple reliefs show her killing enemy kings at Kadesh in person
questions.explanation: Evidence such as a graffito at Sehel near Aswan, left by an official named Ti, and damaged texts in Senenmut's tomb refers to fighting in Nubia during her reign. Megiddo came after her death, under Thutmose III as sole ruler.

questions.stem: As king, Hatshepsut took the throne name:
options: Menkheperre
Nebmaatre
Usermaatre
Maatkare
questions.explanation: Maatkare means roughly 'Truth (Ma'at) is the soul of Ra'. Menkheperre was Thutmose III, Nebmaatre was Amenhotep III and Usermaatre was Ramesses II.

questions.stem: Early statues of Hatshepsut as king show her with a female body, while later ones show a male body, kilt and false beard. The most likely reason for the change is that:
options: the role of king had male imagery, which she adopted to rule fully as pharaoh
she wished to hide from her subjects the fact that she was a woman
her officials had begun the statues before she was crowned and changed them
male statues were cheaper, since they used less stone than female ones
questions.explanation: Her inscriptions still often use feminine grammar, so she was not hiding her sex. Kingship was expressed through male conventions, and she took them on to show she held the office in full.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's inscriptions often mix feminine word endings with the traditional male titles of a king. What does this suggest about how she presented herself?
options: She ruled only as queen and never claimed the titles of a king
She intended her daughter Neferure to rule jointly in her place
She ruled as a woman holding an office that had always been male
Her scribes were careless and copied old texts without reading them
questions.explanation: Monuments call her 'daughter of Ra' as well as 'Horus' and 'King of Upper and Lower Egypt'. The mix reflects a woman adapting a male office, not confusion or a claim only to queenship.

questions.stem: Senenmut, one of Hatshepsut's most powerful officials, held offices that included:
options: steward of Amun and tutor of the princess Neferure
vizier of Lower Egypt and commander of the chariotry
viceroy of Kush and overseer of the gold mines
high priest of Ptah at Memphis and royal physician
questions.explanation: Senenmut was steward of Amun and of the queen, and block statues show him holding Neferure as her tutor. His many titles show how Hatshepsut relied on loyal officials.

questions.stem: Hapuseneb, who served Hatshepsut as High Priest of Amun and also held high civil office, shows that she:
options: removed priests from government and ruled through the army alone
appointed only her relatives to the highest posts in the land
took the office of High Priest of Amun for herself and then for her daughter
bound the Amun priesthood and the administration to her through key men
questions.explanation: By giving offices in both temple and state to supporters such as Hapuseneb and Senenmut, Hatshepsut secured backing from the most powerful institutions of Thebes.

questions.stem: Senenmut had his image carved discreetly in Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahri, and he disappears from the record before the end of her reign. Why is it unwise to claim, as some early Egyptologists did, that he was her lover?
options: Senenmut died before Hatshepsut became king, so they never met
No reliable evidence shows it; the idea rests mainly on later assumptions
Egyptian law forbade any official from being shown inside a royal temple building
Senenmut was her half-brother and could not have married her
questions.explanation: The romance theory grew from Senenmut's unusual prominence and a crude graffito of uncertain meaning. Most historians now treat it as speculation rather than fact.

questions.stem: During Hatshepsut's reign, Thutmose III:
options: ruled Lower Egypt from Memphis as a rival king in the north
was held prisoner in the temple of Amun at Karnak by the priests
appeared on monuments as co-ruler and gained military experience
lived in exile in Nubia until he returned to overthrow her
questions.explanation: Thutmose III's name and image appear alongside Hatshepsut's, as junior co-ruler. Soon after her death he led the campaign that ended at Megiddo, suggesting he had built up military command under her.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's names and images were cut from many monuments, and some of her obelisks were walled in. The evidence shows this began late in Thutmose III's reign, about twenty years after her death. What does the timing suggest?
options: The priests of Amun ordered it because she had closed their temples
The motive was more likely the succession of his son than personal revenge
Thutmose III attacked her monuments as soon as she died out of hatred
The damage was done by tomb robbers looking for gold leaf on the stone
questions.explanation: If Thutmose III hated her, he would probably have acted at once. Many historians think he wished to remove a female king from the record and secure the throne for his son Amenhotep II.

questions.stem: Thutmose III's agents removed Hatshepsut's images as king, but often left those showing her as queen. Which conclusion does this best support?
options: The target was her kingship, the idea of a woman as pharaoh, not her memory
The workers ran out of time and so only damaged the largest and most visible images
Her images as queen were carved in harder stone that could not be cut
Thutmose III wished to keep the record of her marriage to Thutmose II
questions.explanation: The selective damage suggests the aim was to rewrite the royal line, removing a female king, rather than wiping out every trace of her.

questions.stem: Which evidence is the most useful for studying Hatshepsut's reign?
options: Her letters to the kings of Mitanni, found in the archive at Amarna in Middle Egypt
An account by Herodotus, who interviewed members of her court
Her own monuments, such as Deir el-Bahri, and those of her officials
A full biography written by a priest during her own lifetime
questions.explanation: Most evidence for Hatshepsut comes from temples, statues, inscriptions and tombs. No biography survives, the Amarna letters belong to the reigns of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, and Herodotus wrote about a thousand years later.

questions.stem: Why does Hatshepsut not appear in the Ramesside king lists carved at Abydos and Saqqara?
options: Her name was spelled in a foreign script that the scribes could not read
The lists were carved before she was born, under the Middle Kingdom
Later kings left her out because they did not treat her as a legitimate ruler
She ruled for only a few months, much too briefly to be recorded in the official lists
questions.explanation: The Ramesside king lists move from Thutmose II to Thutmose III, omitting her, as they omit the Amarna kings. That reflects later views of legitimacy, not the length of her reign of about two decades.

questions.stem: A historian uses the Deir el-Bahri reliefs as evidence of Hatshepsut's reign. What is the main limitation of this source?
options: It is royal propaganda that presents only what she wished to be remembered
It was carved after her death by Thutmose III to criticise her rule
It covers only her early years as queen and says nothing at all about her reign as king
It is too damaged for any of its scenes or texts to be read today
questions.explanation: The temple was built to honour Amun and to justify her rule, so it shows divine birth, Punt and festivals and leaves out opposition or failure. Many scenes were damaged later but much can still be read.

questions.stem: In 2007 a mummy from tomb KV60 was announced as Hatshepsut's, partly by matching a tooth found in a box bearing her name. How should students treat this identification?
options: As irrelevant, since Hatshepsut's body was known to have been burnt
As possible but debated, since later study questioned the tooth match
As certain, since DNA tests on the tooth confirmed it beyond doubt
As disproved, since the mummy was shown to be a man of the Ramesside era
questions.explanation: The identification was widely reported, but later work questioned whether the tooth fitted the jaw, and DNA testing of the tooth was not carried out. It is best treated as an open question.

questions.stem: Some Egyptologists of the early twentieth century described Hatshepsut as an ambitious usurper who pushed aside Thutmose III. How do many modern historians view her?
options: As a failed ruler whose reign left Egypt poorer and weaker than before
As a myth, since no monuments from her reign have survived to today
As a capable ruler who kept power through a co-regency and loyal officials
As a puppet of Senenmut, who held all real power during her reign
questions.explanation: Modern scholars stress that her reign was prosperous, with major building and trade, and that Thutmose III remained co-ruler. The 'usurper' picture reflected assumptions about women and power.

questions.stem: Which judgement of Hatshepsut's impact is best supported by the evidence?
options: Her building and trade strengthened Thebes and Amun, and later kings built on them
Her reign ended the New Kingdom and began the long and divided Third Intermediate Period
She moved the capital to Amarna and closed the temples of the old gods
She left no lasting monuments, since all her buildings were demolished
questions.explanation: Deir el-Bahri, her work at Karnak and the wealth given to Amun shaped Thebes for centuries, and Thutmose III continued her building at Karnak. The Amarna move was Akhenaten's, over a century later.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahri was partly restored and studied in the twentieth century by Polish archaeologists. Why does archaeology matter so much for interpreting her?
options: Her monuments were damaged and scattered, so reconstruction recovers lost evidence
Archaeologists found her complete diary inside the temple's foundation deposits
Excavation proved that the Punt expedition never took place at all
Archaeology is the only way to learn the names of her parents
questions.explanation: Because her images were defaced and blocks reused, as with the Red Chapel, much evidence has been pieced back together by excavation and reconstruction. Her parents are named in her own inscriptions.

questions.stem: A student argues that Hatshepsut's reign shows women could rule Egypt as easily as men. Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: The claim is correct, since the king lists honour her as a great pharaoh
Her reign shows a woman could rule, but she needed special claims and male imagery
The claim is correct, since several women before her had ruled for decades unopposed
The claim is wrong, since she never held the titles of a king at any time
questions.explanation: Hatshepsut ruled successfully, yet she relied on divine birth, her father's supposed choice and male royal imagery, and her kingship was later erased. Female kings were very rare, and she does appear with full royal titles.
